verses.zh: 提阿非罗大人哪，有好些人提笔作书，述说在我们中间所成就的事，是照传道的人从起初亲眼看见又传给我们的。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] many have undertaken to compile an account[NOTE:2] of the things[NOTE:3] that have been fulfilled[NOTE:4] among us,
notes: Grk “Since” or “Because.” This begins a long sentence that extends through v. 4. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, the Greek sentence has been divided up into shorter English sentences in the translation.

This is sometimes translated “narrative,” but the term itself can refer to an oral or written account. It is the verb “undertaken” which suggests a written account, since it literally is “to set one’s hand” to something (BDAG 386 s.v. ἐπιχειρέω). “Narrative” is too specific, denoting a particular genre of work for the accounts that existed in the earlier tradition. Not all of that material would have been narrative.
Or “events.”

Or “have been accomplished.” Given Luke’s emphasis on divine design (e.g., Luke 24:43-47) a stronger sense (“fulfilled”) is better than a mere reference to something having taken place (“accomplished”).
verses.commentary:
1:1-4 This is one long involved Greek sentence.

1:1

NASB, NKJV
"In as much as"

NRSV, Peshitta
"Since"

NJB
"Seeing that"

The Greek word epeidēper is used only here in the NT. It is not used
at all in the Septuagint, but is used in the Koine papyri found in the garbage dumps of Egypt
(see James Moulton and George Milligan, The Vocabulary of the Greek Testament). It basically
means "since indeed" or "considering that." Luke is setting out the reason he is writing an account
of Jesus' life when there are several already in existence. This probably includes Mark's Gospel
(which forms the literary outline of much of Matthew and Luke), as well as "Q" (a supposed list of
the sayings of Jesus used by both Matthew and Luke). It also implies that by the A.D.
60s there were several written accounts of Jesus' life circulating in the churches.

NASB, REB
"an account"

NKJV
"a narrative"

NRSV
"an orderly account"

TEV
"a report"

NJB
"accounts"

Peshitta
"the story"

This is another Greek term (diēgēsis) found only here in the NT.
It is used twice in the Septuagint in Judges (cf. Judges 5:14; 7:15) for a scribe recording something.
In Greek literature it has the connotation of a full and complete narrative. Luke is describing the
careful, historical research of Jesus' life that preceded his own writing (cf. Luke 1:3).

NASB
"the things accomplished"

NKJV
"those things which are most surely believed"

NRSV
"the events which have been fulfilled"

TEV
"the things that have taken place"

NJB
"events that have reached their fulfilment"

Peshitta
"those works with which we are familiar"

This VERB is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, which
denotes the abiding results of the fulfilled promises concerning Jesus, His teachings, His actions,
and His death and resurrection. The PASSIVE VOICE surely implies that God the Father's
eternal purposes were fully accomplished in Christ.

The term plērophoreō has a dual connotation.

- Paul uses it for being fully persuaded in Rom. 4:21; 14:5; Col. 2:2; 4:12 (cf. NKJV).

- The Papyri uses it of "accomplished" or "fully completed" (cf. NASB, NRSV, NJB).

Theophilus needs to accept both connotations! The OT promises have come to completion in Jesus
of Nazareth.

verses.zh: a
verses.en: like the accounts[NOTE:1] passed on[NOTE:2] to us by those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word[NOTE:3] from the beginning.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “even as”; this compares the recorded tradition of 1:1 with the original eyewitness tradition of 1:2.
Or “delivered.”

The phrase eyewitnesses and servants of the word refers to a single group of people who faithfully passed on the accounts about Jesus. The language about delivery (passed on) points to accounts faithfully passed on to the early church.

Grk “like the accounts those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word passed on to us.” The location of “in the beginning” in the Greek shows that the tradition is rooted in those who were with Jesus from the start.
verses.commentary:
1:2 "they were handed down to us" This is the Greek word paradidōmi, often translated
"traditions" (cf. Mark 7:3,5,8,9,13; 1 Cor. 11:2,23; 15:3). Luke is asserting that he had received information
about the life of Jesus from eyewitnesses. This implies

- the accuracy of his accounts

- the admission that he was a second-generation believer

▣ "those who from the beginning" This refers to a larger number of people beyond the
Twelve Apostles. Some examples would be

- the women who followed Jesus and the Apostles (cf. Luke 8:2-3)

- the one hundred and twenty disciples in the upper room on the day of Pentecost (cf. Acts 1:15)

- the several men to choose from in replacing Judas (cf. Luke 1:21-22)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ARCHĒ

NASB, NRSV
"servants of the word"

NKJV, NJB
"ministers of the word"

TEV
"who proclaimed the message"

REB
"servants of the gospel"

Peshitta
"ministers of the very word"

These "from the beginning" eyewitnesses were responsible proclaimers of the gospel
(cf. 1 Cor. 4:1). To know truth is to be a steward of that truth (cf. 1 Cor. 4:1,2; Titus 1:7; 1 Pet. 4:10)!

The term logos (word) is used of Jesus Himself in John 1:1, but here (cf. Luke 8:12)
and in Acts 6:4; 8:4; 10:36; 11:19; 14:25 it refers to the gospel about Jesus.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW AND GREEK BACKGROUND OF LOGOS

verses.zh: 这些事我既从起头都详细考察了，就定意要按着次序写给你，
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] it seemed good to me as well,[NOTE:2] because I have followed[NOTE:3] all things carefully from the beginning, to write an orderly account[NOTE:4] for you, most excellent Theophilus,
notes: The conjunction “so” is supplied here to bring out the force of the latter part of this Greek sentence, which the translation divides up because of English style. Luke, in compiling his account, is joining a tradition with good precedent.

When Luke says it seemed good to me as well he is not being critical of the earlier accounts, but sees himself stepping into a tradition of reporting about Jesus to which he will add uniquely a second volume on the early church when he writes the Book of Acts.
Grk “having followed”; the participle παρηκολουθηκότι (parēkolouthēkoti) has been translated causally.

An orderly account does not necessarily mean that all events are recorded in the exact chronological sequence in which they occurred, but that the account produced is an orderly one. This could include, for example, thematic or topical order rather than strict chronological order.
verses.commentary:
1:3 This verse is the main clause of verses 1-4 and has several key terms that relate to Luke's research
method.

- "having investigated." This is a PERFECT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE of a word that means
"to follow." The figurative usage of this word meant "to make an extensive effort to learn
the details and truth about something" (See Louw and Nida, Greek-English Lexicon,
vol. 1, p. 331 and Josephus, Against Apion 1.10).

- "carefully." This is the Greek term akribōs, which is translated "accurately,"
"diligently," or "precisely" (cf. Josephus Against Apion 1.10). Louw and Nida,
vol. 1, p. 674, "pertaining to strict conformity to a norm or standard; involving both
detail and completeness." It is used several times in the Septuagint (cf. Deut. 19:18;
Dan. 7:19). Possibly the most relevant usage is that this term was used by Galen (a physician)
for the careful checking of symptoms.

- "from the beginning." This means from the source. In this case

- the beginning events of John's and Jesus' births

- the eyewitnesses from the beginning of Jesus' ministry (i.e., the Apostles, cf. Acts 1:21-22).

- "in consecutive order." This term means "in a continual order," "successively," or "consecutively."

Luke is piling up word after word describing his faithful, accurate, and sequential arrangement
of facts about Jesus' life and ministry. His account is not a fabrication, propaganda, or exaggeration.

▣ "most excellent" This is a first century title of honor and respect. This man may have been
Luke's literary patron. The title is used in Acts of Felix (Acts 23:26; 24:3) and Festus (Acts 26:25), who were
Roman regional officials. It is also used in the Septuagint as "best" (cf. 1 Sam. 15:15; Ps. 15:6; 22:5)
or "chief" (cf. Amos 6:2), but not of people.

▣ "Theophilus" This was a common name in the Mediterranean area, used of both Jews and Gentiles.
Theo means God, plus philos which means

- loved, thus "God lover," "loved by God"

- friend, thus, "friend of God"

▣ "carefully investigated" This is also a medical term used by Galen to denote the careful checking
of symptoms.

verses.zh: 使你知道所学之道都是确实的。
verses.en: so that you may know for certain[NOTE:1] the things you were taught.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “know the truth about”; or “know the certainty of.” The issue of the context is psychological confidence; Luke’s work is trying to encourage Theophilus. So in English this is better translated as “know for certain” than “know certainty” or “know the truth,” which sounds too cognitive. “Certain” assumes the truth of the report. On this term, see Acts 2:36; 21:34; 22:30; 25:26. The meaning “have assurance concerning” is also possible here.

Or “you heard about.” This term can refer merely to a report of information (Acts 21:24) or to instruction (Acts 18:25). The scope of Luke’s Gospel as a whole, which calls for perseverance in the faith and which assumes much knowledge of the OT, suggests Theophilus had received some instruction and was probably a believer.
verses.commentary:
1:4 "in order" This is a PURPOSE CLAUSE (hina with the SUBJUNCTIVE).

▣ "so that you may know" This is an intensified form (epiginōskō) which usually
denotes full and complete knowledge by experience. It may well imply that Theophilus already knew something
of the gospel.

▣ "the things" This is the Greek word logos, which has a wide semantic range. In Luke 1:2
it refers to (1) the truths about Jesus (cf. Luke 7:17) recorded by Luke or (2) the content of what
Theophilus has been taught. This may be an additional evidence he was a new believer (although we must be
careful of reading too much into the words of this introduction which only much later take on a technical
usage in the church).

▣ "taught" From this Greek word we get the English "catechism." This may imply that Theophilus
was a new convert, but this is uncertain because the word is a general, common term.

NASB
"the exact truth about the things"

NKJV
"the certainty of those things"

NRSV
"the truth concerning the things"

TEV
"the full truth about everything"

NJB
"how well founded the teaching is"

Peshitta
"the truth of the words"

The term asphaleia is used in two related senses in the Koine Greek Paypri found in Egypt:

- safety, security

- certainty as to a belief

Luke is trying to reassure Theophilus, his first century readers, and later readers of his
diligence and accuracy as a researcher and Gospel author. Luke's presentation is accurate and trustworthy.
Believers can fully rely on God, on Christ, on Luke's Gospel!

verses.zh: 当犹太王希律的时候，亚比雅班里有一个祭司，名叫撒迦利亚；他妻子是亚伦的后人，名叫伊利莎白。
verses.en: During the reign[NOTE:1] of Herod[NOTE:2] king of Judea, there lived a priest named Zechariah who belonged to[NOTE:3] the priestly division of Abijah,[NOTE:4] and he had a wife named Elizabeth,[NOTE:5] who was a descendant of Aaron.[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “It happened that in the days.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Herod was Herod the Great, who ruled Palestine from 37 b.c. until he died in 4 b.c. He was known for his extensive building projects (including the temple in Jerusalem) and for his cruelty.
Grk “of,” but the meaning of the preposition ἐκ (ek) is more accurately expressed in contemporary English by the relative clause “who belonged to.”
There were twenty-four divisions of priesthood and the priestly division of Abijah was eighth on the list according to 1 Chr 24:10.
Grk “and her name was Elizabeth.”
Grk “a wife of the daughters of Aaron.”sn It was not unusual for a priest to have a wife from a priestly family (a descendant of Aaron); this was regarded as a special blessing.
verses.commentary:
1:5 "Herod" This refers to Herod the Great (37-4 B.C.), an Idumean (from Edom), who,
through political maneuvering and the support of Mark Antony, managed to be appointed ruler of a large part
of Palestine (Canaan) by the Roman Senate in 40 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEROD THE GREAT

▣ "Zechariah" His name meant "remembered by YHWH" (BDB 272). This was John the Baptist's father.

▣ "the division of Abijah" Only four of the twenty-four divisions of Levites returned from the Exile
(cf. 1 Chr. 24:7-18; 2 Chr. 23:8). They were then sub-divided (cf. Ezra 2:36-39) so that different ones
officiated at the temple on different weeks. The Abijah division was considered to be the least prestigious
of the divisions. For a complete discussion of the priestly divisions see Encyclopaedia Judaica,
vol. 12, pp. 89-93.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVITICAL PRIESTS

▣ "he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron" His wife, Elizabeth, was also from a priestly family.
Her Hebrew name (Elizabeth) could mean

- "God is swearer"

- "God fully satisfies"

verses.zh: 他们二人在　神面前都是义人，遵行主的一切诫命礼仪，没有可指摘的，
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] were both righteous in the sight of God, following[NOTE:2] all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “And they.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

Grk “walking in” (an idiom for one’s lifestyle).sn The description of Zechariah and Elizabeth as following…blamelessly was not to say that they were sinless, but that they were faithful and pious. Thus a practical righteousness is meant here (Gen 6:8; Deut 28:9).
The predicate adjective has the effect of an adverb here (BDF §243).
verses.commentary:
1:6 "they were both righteous in the sight of God" "Righteous" is used in this context like Matthew's
definition (cf. Matt. 6:1), not Paul's (cf. Romans 4). This does not imply sinlessness, but someone who
faithfully responds to their understanding of God's will and ways (cf. Deut. 6:25). Old Testament examples
are Noah, Gen. 6:9; 7:1 and Job, Job 1:1. This phrase is included to show that this couple was experiencing
childlessness because of physical problems, not spiritual ones.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

verses.zh: 只是没有孩子；因为伊利莎白不生育，两个人又年纪老迈了。
verses.en: But they did not have a child because Elizabeth was barren,[NOTE:1] and they were both very old.[NOTE:2]
notes: Elizabeth was barren. Both Zechariah and Elizabeth are regarded by Luke as righteous in the sight of God, following all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly (v. 6). With this language, reminiscent of various passages in the OT, Luke is probably drawing implicit comparisons to the age and barrenness of such famous OT personalities as Abraham and Sarah (see, e.g., Gen 18:9-15), the mother of Samson (Judg 13:2-5), and Hannah, the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1-20). And, as it was in the case of these OT saints, so it is with Elizabeth: After much anguish and seeking the Lord, she too is going to have a son in her barrenness. In that day it was a great reproach to be childless, for children were a sign of God’s blessing (cf. Gen 1:28; Lev 20:20-21; Pss 127 and 128; Jer 22:30). As the dawn of salvation draws near, however, God will change this elderly couple’s grief into great joy and grant them the one desire time had rendered impossible.
Grk “were both advanced in days” (an idiom for old age).
verses.commentary:
1:7 Barrenness was considered a divine curse in Jewish culture (cf. Gen. 20:18; 29:31; 30:2; Exod. 23:26;
Lev. 20:20-21; Deut. 7:14; 1 Sam. 1:5; Jer. 22:30). There are several barren women mentioned in the Bible:

- Sarah, Gen. 11:30; 16:1

- Rebekah, Gen. 25:21

- Rachel, Gen. 29:31; 30:1

- Manoah's wife, Jdgs. 13:2,3

- Hannah, 1 Sam. 1:2,5

Not only was Elizabeth barren, but now she was past the time of conception (like Sarah). This
condition is theologically used as a way of asserting God's direct control in the affairs of men. This was
not a virgin birth, but a birth with supernatural assistance.

- like Isaac, cf. Genesis 18

- like Joseph, cf. Gen. 30:22-24

- like Samson, cf. Judges 13

- like Samuel, cf. 1 Samuel 1

- like Hezekiah, Isa. 7:14-16)

John the Baptist will fulfill Old Testament prophecy about the one who would prepare the way for the Messiah
(cf. Isaiah 40 and Malachi 3).

verses.zh: 撒迦利亚按班次在　神面前供祭司的职分，
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] while Zechariah[NOTE:2] was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty,[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “Now it happened that.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “he”; the referent (Zechariah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “serving as priest in the order of his division before God.”sn Zechariah’s division would be on duty twice a year for a week at a time.
verses.commentary:
1:8 "while he was performing his priestly service before God" The Mishnah (part of the Talmud) says there
were so many priests at this time that each offered incense only once in his lifetime; others, not at all.

verses.zh: 照祭司的规矩掣签，得进主殿烧香。
verses.en: he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood,[NOTE:1] to enter[NOTE:2] the Holy Place[NOTE:3] of the Lord and burn incense.
notes: Grk “according to the custom of the priesthood it fell to him by lot.” The order of the clauses has been rearranged in the translation to make it clear that the prepositional phrase κατὰ τὸ ἔθος τῆς ἱερατείας (kata to ethos tēs hierateias, “according to the custom of the priesthood”) modifies the phrase “it fell to him by lot” rather than the preceding clause.
This is an aorist participle and is temporally related to the offering of incense, not to when the lot fell.

Or “temple.” Such sacrifices, which included the burning of incense, would have occurred in the holy place according to the Mishnah (m. Tamid 1.2; 3.1; 5-7). A priest would have given this sacrifice, which was offered for the nation, once in one’s career. It would be offered either at 9 a.m. or 3 p.m., since it was made twice a day.

gr.gloss: it fell to him by lot

verses.commentary:
1:9 "he was chosen by lot" Lots were a mechanical way to determine the will of God (cf Acts 1:21-26).
There were several priests on duty at one time. This was the regular way to determine which offered the ritual.

In the OT the "lot" originally referred to the Urim and Thummim (cf. Lev. 16:8), which was
carried behind the breastplate of the High Priest. It was a mechanical way of determining the will of God,
usually for the King.

It was used as a way to divide the Promised Land among the tribes in Joshua 13-19.

The casting of lots was used by the early church to choose a new apostle to replace Judas
in Acts 1:21-26.

SPECIAL TOPIC: URIM AND THUMMIM

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREASTPLATE OF THE HIGH PRIEST

▣ "to burn the incense" This procedure is described in Exod. 25:6; 30:7; 31:11. The incense itself
is described in Exod. 30:34-38.

verses.zh: 烧香的时候，众百姓在外面祷告。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] the whole crowd[NOTE:2] of people were praying[NOTE:3] outside at the hour of the incense offering.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “And,” but “now” better represents the somewhat parenthetical nature of this statement in the flow of the narrative.

Grk “all the multitude.” While “assembly” is sometimes used here to translate πλῆθος (plēthos), that term usually implies in English a specific or particular group of people. However, this was simply a large group gathered outside, which was not unusual, especially for the afternoon offering.

The plural verb is used here on the probability that the crowd acted as individuals, each person praying on their own but at the same time. English versions are divided on how they handle this; see, e.g., NRSV, HCSB, which have the singular verb “was praying.”
The “hour of the incense offering” is another way to refer to the time of sacrifice.
verses.commentary:
1:10 Obviously this was a set time of prayer associated with the sacrifice of the Continual (a twice
daily sacrifice and burnt offering of two lambs) at 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. Jewish sources advocate the offering of
incense twice a day in connection to "the Continual" sacrifice (cf. Exod. 30:7-8). Incense burning with much smoke
was a physical symbol of prayer rising to God.

verses.zh: 有主的使者站在香坛的右边，向他显现。
verses.en: An[NOTE:1] angel of the Lord,[NOTE:2] standing on the right side of the altar of incense, appeared[NOTE:3] to him.
notes: Grk “And an angel.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, δέ (de) has not been translated here.

Or “the angel of the Lord.” Linguistically, “angel of the Lord” is the same in both testaments (and thus, he is either “an angel of the Lord” or “the angel of the Lord” in both testaments). For arguments and implications, see ExSyn 252; M. J. Davidson, “Angels,” DJG, 9; W. G. MacDonald argues for “an angel” in both testaments: “Christology and ‘The Angel of the Lord’,” Current Issues in Biblical and Patristic Interpretation, 324-35.
This term is often used to describe a supernatural appearance (24:34; Acts 2:3; 7:2, 30, 35; 9:17; 13:31; 16:9; 26:16).
verses.commentary:
1:11 "an angel of the Lord" This phrase is used two ways in the OT.

- an angel (cf. Gen. 24:7,40; Exod. 23:20-23; 32:34; Num. 22:22; Jdgs. 5:23; 1 Sam. 24:16; 1 Chr. 21:15ff;
Zech. 1:28)

- as a way of referring to a physical manifestation of YHWH (cf. Gen. 16:7-13; 22:11-15; 31:11,13;
48:15-16; Exod. 3:2,4; 13:21; 14:19; Jdgs. 2:1; 6:22-24; 13:3-23; Zech. 3:1-2).

Luke uses the phrase often (cf. Luke 1:11,13; 2:9; Acts 5:19; 7:30; 8:26; 12:7,11,23; 10:3; 27:23)
in the sense of #1 above. The NT does not use sense #2, "an angel of the Lord,"
unless Acts 18:26 and 29 is in a reference to the Holy Spirit.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD

▣ "standing to the right of the altar of incense" The altar of incense was located in the Holy
Place, next to the veil of the Holy of Holies. The description of this golden incense altar is found in
Exod. 30:1-10. This would place the angel between the incense altar and the seven pointed candle stand (Menorah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF INCENSE

SPECIAL TOPIC: VEIL, I. C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAMPSTAND

verses.zh: 撒迦利亚看见，就惊慌害怕。
verses.en: And Zechariah, visibly shaken when he saw the angel,[NOTE:1] was seized with fear.[NOTE:2]
notes: The words “the angel” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects were frequently omitted in Greek when clear from the context.
Or “and he was afraid”; Grk “fear fell upon him.” Fear is common when supernatural agents appear (1:29-30, 65; 2:9; 5:8-10; 9:34; 24:38; Exod 15:16; Judg 6:22-23; 13:6, 22; 2 Sam 6:9).
verses.commentary:
1:12 Fear is the common human response in the presence of the spiritual realm (cf. Gen. 15:1; 21:17;
Exod. 14:13,31; Josh. 8:1; 10:8; Dan. 10:12,19; Rev. 1:17). However, again and again the divine message is
a clear "fear not" (cf. Luke 1:13,30; 2:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT), B.

verses.zh: 天使对他说：「撒迦利亚，不要害怕，因为你的祈祷已经被听见了。你的妻子伊利莎白要给你生一个儿子，你要给他起名叫约翰。
verses.en: But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard,[NOTE:1] and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son; you[NOTE:2] will name him John.[NOTE:3]
notes: The passive means that the prayer was heard by God.sn Your prayer has been heard. Zechariah’s prayer while offering the sacrifice would have been for the nation, but the answer to the prayer also gave them a long hoped-for child, a hope they had abandoned because of their old age.
Grk “a son, and you”; καί (kai) has not been translated. Instead a semicolon is used in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Grk “you will call his name John.” The future tense here functions like a command (see ExSyn 569-70). This same construction occurs in v. 31.sn “Do not be afraid…you must call his name John.” This is a standard birth announcement (see Gen 16:11; Isa 7:14; Matt 1:21; Luke 1:31).
verses.commentary:
1:13 "Do not be afraid" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) IMPERATIVE with
the NEGATIVE PARTICLE, which usually means stop an act already in progress. We get the English
term "phobia" from this Greek term (phobos).

▣ "your petition has been heard" Zacharias was still praying for a child. The incense he was offering
to God was a symbol of prayer. In Zacharias' priestly circle the offering of incense was considered a great
honor. It was also considered to be a special time for personal requests.

▣ "John" In Hebrew (Yohanan) it means "one whom God has graciously given" or
"YHWH is gracious" (BDB 220).

verses.zh: 你必欢喜快乐；有许多人因他出世，也必喜乐。
verses.en: Joy and gladness will come[NOTE:1] to you, and many will rejoice at[NOTE:2] his birth,[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “This will be joy and gladness.”
Or “because of.”
“At his birth” is more precise as the grammatical subject (1:58), though “at his coming” is a possible force, since it is his mission, as the following verses note, that will really bring joy.
verses.commentary:
1:14 John's birth will be a blessing, not only to Zacharias and his family, but to Israel and, by
implication, to all the earth.

verses.zh: 他在主面前将要为大，淡酒浓酒都不喝，从母腹里就被圣灵充满了。
verses.en: for he will be great in the sight of[NOTE:1] the Lord. He[NOTE:2] must never drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “before.”
Grk “and he”; because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun in the translation.

Huge numbers of spiritually hungry Jews flocked to him.

notes: Grk “before him”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

These two lines cover all relationships: Turn the hearts of the fathers back to their children points to horizontal relationships, while (turn) the disobedient to the wisdom of the just shows what God gives from above in a vertical manner.
verses.commentary:
1:17 "in the spirit and power of Elijah" This verse is an allusion to the prophecies of Mal. 3:1 and
4:5-6. Elijah was to precede the Messiah. However, John fills the role of Elijah (cf. Matt. 11:14; 17:10-13).
The fact that John fulfills the Elijah prophecies should warn us about western literalsim! See D. Brent Sandy,
Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

As Elisha received the Spirit of Elijah to become a prophet (cf. 1 Kgs. 19:16), Elisha asks
for a double portion of Elijah's spirit (cf. 2 Kgs. 2:9). In a sense Elisha continued the ministry of Elijah.
This is what John does; he extends the eschatological ministry of Elijah foretold in Malachi 3 and 4.

notes: Grk “And Zechariah.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “How will I know this?”
Grk “is advanced in days” (an idiom for old age).
verses.commentary:
1:18 "How will I know" This sounds very much like Abraham (cf. Gen. 15:8) and Mary (cf. Luke 1:34).
However, apparently God knows the heart, he asked in a doubting way to which God reacted (cf. Matt. 12:38;
16:1; Mark 8:11-12; John 2:18; 6:30; 1 Cor. 1:22). Modern interpreters are not able to do psychoanalysis
on biblical characters!

notes: Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “the one who is standing before God.”
Grk “to announce these things of good news to you.”
verses.commentary:
1:19 "Gabriel" This Hebrew name means "God's strong man," "man of God," or "God is my warrior" (BDB 150).
This is God's messenger angel (cf. Luke 1:26; Dan. 8:16; 9:21). There are only two angels named in the Bible:

- Gabriel, who is God's messenger angel to Daniel, Zacharias, and Mary

- Michael (BDB 567), who is the Israel's national archangel (cf. Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1; Jude 9; Rev. 12:7); He is also
called an archangel in Jude v. 9 and a prince in Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "who stands in the presence of God" Angeology became a major element of rabbinical theology and
speculation following Israel's contact with Zoroastrianism in the Babylonian exile (dualistic Persian religion). The Bible is
silent and vague about the spiritual realm. What is presented is often in figurative language or symbols. From the OT
there are two types of angels surrounding YHWH's throne-Seraphim (cf. Isaiah 6) and Cherubim
(cf. Ezekiel 1; 10).

Gabriel's authority rests on his relationship with and proximity to God. This is an important
message from God for His purposes (i.e., good news in fallen, alienated humans).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERAPHIM

notes: Grk “behold.”
The predicted fulfillment in the expression my words, which will be fulfilled in their time takes place in Luke 1:63-66.
Silent, unable to speak. Actually Zechariah was deaf and mute as 1:61-63 indicates, since others had to use gestures to communicate with him.
verses.commentary:
1:20 This verse serves as a powerful warning about rejecting, or at least not fully believing, a
message from God. Humans may fear the spiritual realm (angels, see note at 1:12), but they must respect
their message! The consequences of rejection are potent.

"But now"

"to see." For Luke it has become a literary technique to draw attention to a statement (similar to Jesus' "Amen,

verses.zh: 百姓等候撒迦利亚，诧异他许久在殿里。

notes: Grk “And.” Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
The imperfect verb ἐθαύμαζον (ethaumazon) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
Or “temple.” See the note on the phrase “the holy place” in v. 9.
verses.commentary:
1:21 "the temple" This is the term naos. Literally it is from the term "to dwell." It came to
be used of the central shrine made up of the Holy of Holies and the Holy Place.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TABERNACLE OF THE WILDERNESS

verses.zh: 及至他出来，不能和他们说话，他们就知道他在殿里见了异象；因为他直向他们打手式，竟成了哑巴。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he came out, he was not able to speak to them. They[NOTE:2] realized that he had seen a vision[NOTE:3] in the Holy Place[NOTE:4] because[NOTE:5] he was making signs to them and remained unable to speak.[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “And when.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “and they.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
That is, “he had had a supernatural encounter in the holy place,” since the angel came to Zechariah by the altar. This was not just a “mental experience.”
Or “temple.” See the note on the phrase “the holy place” in v. 9.
Grk “and,” but the force is causal or explanatory in context.
Grk “dumb,” but this could be understood to mean “stupid” in contemporary English, whereas the point is that he was speechless.
verses.commentary:
1:22 "when he came out, he was unable to speak" According to rabbinical tradition it was customary
for the priest to bless the people when he came out from burning incense, using the Aaronic blessing of
Num. 6:24-26.

verses.zh: 他供职的日子已满，就回家去了。
verses.en: When his time of service was over,[NOTE:1] he went to his home.
notes: Grk “And it happened that as the days of his service were ended.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

verses.zh: 这些日子以后，他的妻子伊利莎白怀了孕，就隐藏了五个月，
verses.en: After some time[NOTE:1] his wife Elizabeth became pregnant,[NOTE:2] and for five months she kept herself in seclusion.[NOTE:3] She said,[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “After these days.” The phrase refers to a general, unspecified period of time that passes before fulfillment comes.
Or “Elizabeth conceived.”
The text does not state why Elizabeth withdrew into seclusion, nor is the reason entirely clear.
Grk “she kept herself in seclusion, saying.” The participle λέγουσα (legousa) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 说：「主在眷顾我的日子，这样看待我，要把我在人间的羞耻除掉。」
verses.en: “This is what[NOTE:1] the Lord has done for me at the time[NOTE:2] when he has been gracious to me,[NOTE:3] to take away my disgrace[NOTE:4] among people.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “Thus.”
Grk “in the days.”
Grk “has looked on me” (an idiom for taking favorable notice of someone).

Barrenness was often seen as a reproach or disgrace (Lev 20:20-21; Jer 22:30), but now at her late age (the exact age is never given in Luke’s account), God had miraculously removed it (see also Luke 1:7).
Grk “among men,” but the context clearly indicates a generic use of ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) here.
verses.commentary:
1:25 This shows how she felt about being barren. It was viewed as a curse from God (cf. Gen. 30:23). See
full note at Luke 1:7.

verses.zh: 到了第六个月，天使加百列奉　神的差遣往加利利的一座城去（这城名叫拿撒勒），
verses.en: In the sixth month of Elizabeth’s pregnancy,[NOTE:1] the angel Gabriel[NOTE:2] was sent by[NOTE:3] God to a town of Galilee called Nazareth,[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “in the sixth month.” The phrase “of Elizabeth’s pregnancy” was supplied in the translation to clarify the exact time meant by this reference. That Elizabeth’s pregnancy is meant is clear from vv. 24-25.

Gabriel is the same angel mentioned previously in v. 19. He is traditionally identified as an angel who brings revelation (see Dan 8:15-16; 9:21). Gabriel and Michael are the only two good angels named in the Bible.
Or “from.” The account suggests God’s planned direction in these events, so “by” is better than “from,” as six months into Elizabeth’s pregnancy, God acts again.

For location see Map1-D3; Map2-C2; Map3-D5; Map4-C1; Map5-G3.sn Nazareth was a town in the region of Galilee, located north of Samaria and Judea. Galilee extended from about 45 to 85 miles north of Jerusalem and was about 30 miles in width. Nazareth was a very small village and was located about 15 miles west of the southern edge of the Sea of Galilee.
verses.commentary:
1:26 "sixth month" This refers to Elizabeth's pregnancy (cf. Luke 1:36).

▣ "Gabriel" See note at Luke 1:19.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "a city in Galilee called Nazareth" Galilee was known as a Gentile area although many Jews
lived there (apparently a small, new community from the royal tribe of Judah lived in Nazareth). Nazareth
is never mentioned in the OT or the Talmud or by Flavius Josephus. The name Nazareth itself may be related
to the Messianic title "Branch" (nezer, cf. Isa. 11:1; Matt. 2:23). People from this area were generally
looked down upon by Judean Jews. This is related to the prophecy of Isa. 9:1 (see note online at Isaiah 9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

verses.zh: 到一个童女那里，是已经许配大卫家的一个人，名叫约瑟。童女的名字叫马利亚；
verses.en: to a virgin engaged[NOTE:1] to a man whose name was Joseph, a descendant of David,[NOTE:2] and the virgin’s name was Mary.
notes: Or “promised in marriage.”
The Greek word order here favors connecting Davidic descent to Joseph, not Mary, in this remark.tn Grk “Joseph, of the house of David.”
verses.commentary:
1:27 "a virgin" The Greek word from the Septuagint (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT) pathenon is not ambiguous as the Hebrew
Almah (BDB 761 II) is in Isa. 7:4. It specifically means virgin. Matthew and Luke assert that
Jesus had no human father (cf. Luke 1:34), that He was the ultimate fulfillment of Isa. 7:14 and Gen. 3:15!
This child is of God, not of man (i.e., Immanuel). It is surprising that Luke's source does not
mention Isa. 7:14.

Outside of the birth accounts of Matthew and Luke the virgin birth is not specifically
mentioned in the NT. It does not appear in any of the sermons of Acts or the later Epistles. This is
not because it is not true, but because it might be misunderstood by a polytheistic Greek/Roman culture,
which believed that the gods at Olympus regularly took human women and produced offspring. The uniqueness
of the biblical account would be lost in this cultural context.

At this point I wold like to use my comments from Isa. 7:14
(see www.freebiblecommentary.org).

"virgin" The Hebrew term here is almah (BDB 761). This term is used for a
young woman of marriageable age (cf. Gen. 43:24; Exod. 2:8; Pro. 30:19). It designates a woman who is
sexually mature. There is another Hebrew term for virgin, bethulah (BDB 143), which is used by
Isaiah in Isa. 23:4, 12; 37:22; 47:1; 62:5. The Septuagint translates this verse with the Greek term "virgin."
These terms are semantically overlapping and all of the young girls in Israeli culture were considered to
be virgins. However, I do not believe in two virgin births, but one. There was a normal conception in Ahaz's
day as a sign and a ("the," MT) virgin conception in Jesus' day (cf. Matt. 1:18-23; Luke 1:26-38). This is
a multi-fulfillment prophecy!

I think the reason that the NT does not emphasize this more (only appears in the two
birth narratives [i.e., Matt. 1:23; Luke 1:31,34] and never in a sermon in Acts or an Epistle by any Apostle)
is because of the possible misunderstanding of Greco-Roman religion where the cohabitation of gods and humans,
resulting in offspring, was common.

To try to base a doctrine of sin as transmitted through male sperm and, therefore, show
the reason for a virgin birth is, in my opinion, folly! In reality it is similar to the barren wives of the
Patriarchs having children only at God's instigation. God is in control of the Messiah! An even greater truth
is revealed in the NT where the Messiah is presented clearly as incarnated Deity (i.e., John 1:1; 5:18; 10:33;
14:9-11; Phil. 2:6)! Thus the need for a virgin birth!

▣ "engaged" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE. In Jewish culture of the first
century, this was legally binding. Only divorce or death could break this arrangement. Girls became
marriageable at 12 years of age (bat mitzvah) with a one year betrothal period (Ketubot 4.4-5).
For OT background see Deut. 22:23-27.

▣ "Joseph, of the descendants of David" Whether Joseph (BDB 415, meaning "may YHWH add") and Mary
both were of Davidic descent or just Joseph is uncertain (cf. Luke 2:4-5). Mary is said to be a relative of Elizabeth, who was
of the line of Aaron, as was her husband Zacharias (cf. Luke 1:5,36). The issue is significant because of the promises and
prophecies of 2 Sam. 7:12-16; Ps. 89:19ff). The obvious differences between the genealogies of Matthew and Luke are
probably due to different lineages. Many commentators assume that Luke records the royal genealogy of Mary (Jesus' actual
lineage), while Matthew records Joseph's royal lineage (Jesus' Jewish legal lineage). However, this is only speculation.

The very fact the early church knew of these different genealogies and did not try to reconcile
them illustrates the genineness of these historical eyewitness accounts.

▣ "name was Mary" The name "Mary" (Maria, Luke 1:27) has several possible etymologies.

- from Moses sister, Miriam (BDB 599, cf. Exod. 15:21). The meaning of the name is unclear

- Egyptian root ‒ beloved

- Hebrew root (uncertain)

- bitter

- rebellious

- stiff or erect

- sea of bitterness

- strong, thick

- from a women named Naomi (i.e., pleasant, Ruth 1:20). She asked to be called "Mara" (i.e., bitter)

- from Aramaic "Maryam" ‒ Mar-bitter; yam-sea

- from Eusebius and Jerome, from "Mar" (i.e., sea)

- Synoptic Gospels call her "Maria" (cf. Luke 1:27)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARY (several different people)

verses.zh: 天使进去，对她说：「蒙大恩的女子，我问你安，主和你同在了！」
verses.en: The[NOTE:1] angel[NOTE:2] came[NOTE:3] to her and said, “Greetings, favored one,[NOTE:4] the Lord is with you!”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “And coming to her.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “And coming to her, he said”; the referent (the angel) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “coming to her, he said.” The participle εἰσελθών (eiselthōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

The address, “favored one” (a perfect participle, Grk “Oh one who is favored”) points to Mary as the recipient of God’s grace, not a bestower of it. She is a model saint in this passage, one who willingly receives God’s benefits. The Vulgate rendering “full of grace” suggests something more of Mary as a bestower of grace, but does not make sense here contextually.

Most mss (A C D Θ ƒ13 33 M latt sy) read here εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξίν (eulogēmenē su en gunaixin, “blessed are you among women”) which also appears in 1:42 (where it is textually certain). This has the earmarks of a scribal addition for balance; the shorter reading, attested by the most significant witnesses and several others (א B L W Ψ ƒ1 565 579 700 1241 co), is thus preferred.
verses.commentary:
1:28

NASB, REB, NIV, NET
"Greetings"

NRSV, NJB
"rejoice"

TEV
"peace"

Peshitta
"Peace be to you"

This is a form of the normal term for "greeting" (chairein, cf. Acts 15:23; James 1:1)
in the Greco-Roman world of the first century. Its grammatical form is PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE.
Its basic meaning is "be full of joy" or "continue to rejoice." It may reflect the Messianic passage of Zech. 9:9.

There is the added possibility that this term was used in the Septuagint in contexts where
the phrase "do not be afraid" is used and God's people are told to rejoice because God is about to deliver them.

- Lamentations 4:21-22

- Joel 2:21-27

- Zephaniah 3:14-20

- Zechariah 9:9

The angel's first words are a sound play on chaire and kecharitōmenē
(a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE), which is "be glad, favored one." These words have different
etymological roots, but they sound alike. See note below on the second term in the angel's message.

NASB, NRSV, NET
"favored one!"

TEV
"The Lord. . .has greatly blessed you!"

NJB
"you who enjoy God's favour!"

REB
"most favoured one!"

Peshitta
"O full of grace"

Vulgate
"Hail, Mary, full of grace!"

NAB
"Hail, favored one!"

The Vulgate has "Hail, Mary, full of grace." This is a good translation if we see that Mary
is the recipient of God's grace, not the giver of grace (NJB, "you who enjoy God's favor!"). There is only
one mediator, Jesus (cf. 1 Tim. 2:5). However, this was a great and unique honor for a young, peasant woman
(cf. Luke 1:48). This greeting shocked her (cf. Luke 1:29).

▣ "you" There are several ancient Greek uncial manuscripts (MSS A, C, D) which add the phrase
"blessed are you among women." This illustrates one of the recurrent tendencies of the early Christian copyists (i.e., scribes)
to harmonize phrasing (see Luke 1:42). The UBS4 critical apparatus gives the absence of the phrase
(MSS א, B, L, W) in Luke 1:28 an "A" rating (certain).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

verses.zh: 马利亚因这话就很惊慌，又反覆思想这样问安是甚么意思。
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] she was greatly troubled[NOTE:2] by his words and began to wonder about the meaning of this greeting.[NOTE:3]
notes: Most mss (A C Θ 0130 ƒ13 M lat sy) have ἰδοῦσα (idousa, “when [she] saw [the angel]”) here as well, making Mary’s concern the appearance of the angel. This construction is harder than the shorter reading since it adds a transitive verb without an explicit object. However, the shorter reading has significant support (א B D L W Ψ ƒ1 565 579 1241 sa) and on balance should probably be considered authentic.
On the phrase greatly troubled see 1:12. Mary’s reaction was like Zechariah’s response.
Grk “to wonder what kind of greeting this might be.” Luke often uses the optative this way to reveal a figure’s thinking (3:15; 8:9; 18:36; 22:23).

verses.zh: 天使对她说：「马利亚，不要怕！你在　神面前已经蒙恩了。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid,[NOTE:2] Mary, for you have found favor[NOTE:3] with God!
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate that Gabriel’s statement is a response to Mary’s perplexity over the greeting.
Do not be afraid. See 1:13 for a similar statement to Zechariah.
Or “grace.” sn The expression found favor is a Semitism, common in the OT (Gen 6:8; 18:3; 43:14; 2 Sam 15:25). God has chosen to act on this person’s behalf.
verses.commentary:
1:30 "'Do not be afraid'" This is a PRESENT IMPERATIVE with the NEGATIVE PARTICLE
negated, which usually means to stop an act in process.

Humans are often overwhelmed by the power and glory of the spiritual realm and told to "fear not"

- by God Himself

- by God to Abraham ‒ Gen. 15:1; 26:24

- by the Angel of the Lord to Hagar ‒ Gen. 21:17

- by God to Moses ‒ Deut 1:21

- by God to Joshua ‒ Josh. 1:9; 8:1

- by God to Gideon ‒ Jdgs. 6:23

- by God to Israel ‒ Isa. 41:10,13,14; 43:5; 44:2

- by angels

- to Daniel ‒ Dan. 10:12,19

- to Mary ‒ Luke 1:13; 2:10

- Jesus to His followers ‒ Matt. 14:27; 17:7; 28:10; Mark 6:50; Luke 5:10; 12:32; John 6:20; Rev. 1:17

▣ "you have found favor with God" This seems to be an OT idiom for God's special activity in
someone's life (cf. Gen. 6:8; 18:3; 19:19; 30:27; Exod. 33:12,17; Acts 7:46). God chooses to use imperfect,
but available, humans who choose to trust Him to accomplish His purposes in this world (i.e., Exod. 3:7-10).

verses.zh: 你要怀孕生子，可以给他起名叫耶稣。
verses.en: Listen:[NOTE:1] You will become pregnant[NOTE:2] and give birth to[NOTE:3] a son, and you will name him[NOTE:4] Jesus.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “And behold.”
Grk “you will conceive in your womb.”

verses.en: The angel replied,[NOTE:1] “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow[NOTE:2] you. Therefore the child[NOTE:3] to be born[NOTE:4] will be holy;[NOTE:5] he will be called the Son of God.
notes: Grk “And the angel said to her.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style. The pronoun αὐτῇ (autē, “to her”) has not been included in the translation since it is redundant in contemporary English.
The phrase will overshadow is a reference to God’s glorious presence at work (Exod 40:34-35; Ps 91:4).

Or “the one born holy will be called the Son of God.” The wording of this phrase depends on whether the adjective is a predicate adjective, as in the text, or is an adjective modifying the participle serving as the subject. The absence of an article with the adjective speaks for a predicate position. Other less appealing options supply a verb for “holy”; thus “the one who is born will be holy”; or argue that both “holy” and “Son of God” are predicates, so “The one who is born will be called holy, the Son of God.”

A few mss (C* Θ ƒ1 33 pc) add “by you” here. This looks like a scribal addition to bring symmetry to the first three clauses of the angel’s message (note the second person pronoun in the previous two clauses), and is too poorly supported to be seriously considered as authentic.

Or “Therefore the holy child to be born will be called the Son of God.” There are two ways to understand the Greek phrase τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον (to gennōmenon hagion) here. First, τὸ γεννώμενον could be considered a substantival participle with ἅγιον as an adjective in the second predicate position, thus making a complete sentence; this interpretation is reflected in the translation above. Second, τὸ ἅγιον could be considered a substantival adjective with γεννώμενον acting as an adjectival participle, thus making the phrase the subject of the verb κληθήσεται (klēthēsetai); this interpretation is reflected in the alternative reading. Treating the participle γεννώμενον as adjectival is a bit unnatural for the very reason that it forces one to understand ἅγιον as substantival; this introduces a new idea in the text with ἅγιον when an already new topic is being introduced with γεννώμενον. Semantically this would overload the new subject introduced at this point. For this reason the first interpretation is preferred.

"Overshadow" (episkiazō) seems to be related to the OT Shekinah cloud of

The following passage has been typeset as poetry because many scholars regard this passage as poetic or hymnic. These terms are used broadly to refer to the genre of writing, not to the content. There are two broad criteria for determining if a passage is poetic or hymnic: “(a) stylistic: a certain rhythmical lilt when the passages are read aloud, the presence of parallelismus membrorum (i.e., an arrangement into couplets), the semblance of some metre, and the presence of rhetorical devices such as alliteration, chiasmus, and antithesis; and (b) linguistic: an unusual vocabulary, particularly the presence of theological terms, which is different from the surrounding context” (P. T. O’Brien, Philippians [NIGTC], 188-89). Classifying a passage as hymnic or poetic is important because understanding this genre can provide keys to interpretation. However, not all scholars agree that the above criteria are present in this passage, so the decision to typeset it as poetry should be viewed as a tentative decision about its genre.

1:46 "Mary" There is an interesting discussion about which name-(1) Mary, (2) Elizabeth, or (3) no
name at all-appeared in the original autograph. All Greek witnesses have "Mary" (spelled two different ways),
but three Latin texts and comments by Irenaeus and Jerome, commenting on Origen's notes, have given rise to
speculation. For further information, see Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New
Testament, pp. 130-131.

verses.zh: 我灵以　神我的救主为乐；
verses.en: and my spirit has begun to rejoice[NOTE:1] in God my Savior,
notes: Or “rejoices.” The translation renders this aorist, which stands in contrast to the previous line’s present tense, as ingressive, which highlights Mary’s joyous reaction to the announcement. A comprehensive aorist is also possible here.
verses.commentary:
1:47 "God my Savior" Mary recognizes her need for a savior!

As there has been an ambiguity in the use of Lord (kurios), possibly referring to YHWH
or the Messiah, it is interesting to me how this possibly "purposeful" ambiguity continues throughout the NT.
The Trinitarian aspect of God's nature unifies the Father and the Son.

In Paul's letter to Titus he calls the Father "Savior" three times (cf. Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4). In
every context he also calls Jesus "Savior" (cf. Titus 1:4; 2:13; 3:6).

verses.zh: 因为他顾念他使女的卑微；从今以后，万代要称我有福。
verses.en: because he has looked upon the humble state of his servant.[NOTE:1] For[NOTE:2] from now on[NOTE:3] all generations will call me blessed,[NOTE:4]
notes: See the note on the word “servant” in v. 38.
Grk “for behold.”
From now on is a favorite phrase of Luke’s, showing how God’s acts change things from this point on (5:10; 12:52; 22:18, 69; Acts 18:6).
Mary is seen here as an example of an object of God’s grace (blessed) for all generations.
verses.commentary:
1:48 "humble state" God chose a teenaged peasant girl to be the Messiah's mother (cf. Gen. 3:15). Isn’t
that just like God! He is in control. He will be magnified. He does not need human merit or performance. He
will bring redemption! Note the unconditonal covenant of Gen. 15:12-21.

▣ "will call me blessed" Elizabeth has already blessed her younger relative twice (cf. Luke 1:42,45).
This will be repeated throughout time because of the significance of her Son!

notes: Grk “and from.” Here καί (kai) has been translated by a semicolon to improve the English style.
God’s mercy refers to his “loyal love” or “steadfast love,” expressed in faithful actions, as the rest of the psalm illustrates.
That is, “who revere.” This refers to those who show God a reverential respect for his sovereignty.
verses.commentary:

to YHWH's unchanging character of mercy and covenant loyalty toward those who believe (cf. Exod. 34:6; Deut. 5:10;
7:9; Ps. 103:17).

verses.zh: 他用膀臂施展大能；那狂傲的人正心里妄想就被他赶散了。
verses.en: He has demonstrated power[NOTE:1] with his arm; he has scattered those whose pride wells up from the sheer arrogance[NOTE:2] of their hearts.
notes: Or “shown strength,” “performed powerful deeds.” The verbs here switch to aorist tense through 1:55. This is how God will act in general for his people as they look to his ultimate deliverance.

Grk “in the imaginations of their hearts.” The psalm rebukes the arrogance of the proud, who think that power is their sovereign right. Here διανοίᾳ (dianoia) can be understood as a dative of sphere or reference/respect.
verses.commentary:

body. It is used in the Bible to describe God's power to act (cf. Ps. 98:1; 118:15-16; Isa. 51:9; 52:10). Often
Jesus is depicted at the Father's right hand (cf. Matt. 22:44; 26:64; Luke 20:42; 22:69; Acts 2:33,34; 5:31;
7:55,56).

actions in the OT recorded in the Septuagint (cf. Num. 10:35; Deut. 30:1,3; Jer. 51:20-22). God's ways are
so different from mankind's ways (cf. Isa. 55:8-9). He exalts those who are weak, powerless, and humble,

The Greek term for "proud" (huperēphanos) is used often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 1:25;

verses.zh: 他叫有权柄的失位，叫卑贱的升高；
verses.en: He has brought down the mighty[NOTE:1] from their thrones, and has lifted up those of lowly position;[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “rulers.”
Or “those of humble position”sn The contrast between the mighty and those of lowly position is fundamental for Luke. God cares for those that the powerful ignore (Luke 4:18-19).
verses.commentary:
1:52 This is parallel to Luke 1:51, as is Luke 1:53. This is known as a "reversal" promise (i.e.,
unexpected outcome). YHWH will bring down the proud and powerful, but will exalt the lowly!

verses.zh: 叫饥饿的得饱美食，叫富足的空手回去。
verses.en: he has filled the hungry with good things,[NOTE:1] and has sent the rich away empty.[NOTE:2]
notes: Good things refers not merely to material blessings, but blessings that come from knowing God.
Another fundamental contrast of Luke’s is between the hungry and the rich (Luke 6:20-26).
verses.commentary:
1:53 This is a quote from Ps. 107:9. The same concept is found in Ps. 146:7-9. God's ways are not
mankind's ways (cf. Isa. 55:8-11).

verses.zh: 他扶助了他的仆人以色列，
verses.en: He has helped his servant Israel, remembering[NOTE:1] his mercy,[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “because he remembered mercy,” understanding the infinitive as causal.
Or “his [God’s] loyal love.”
verses.commentary:
1:54 "to Israel His servant" The term "servant" was originally used in the OT as an honorific title
for leaders (e.g., Moses, Joshua, David).

It came to be used in a collective sense for Israel, especially in the Servant Songs of Isaiah
(cf. Luke 41:8-9; 42:18-19; 43:10). This collective sense is personified in an ideal Israelite (i.e., the
Messiah in Isa. 42:1; 52:13-53:12).

verses.en: as he promised[NOTE:1] to our ancestors,[NOTE:2] to Abraham and to his descendants[NOTE:3] forever.”
notes: Grk “as he spoke.” Since this is a reference to the covenant to Abraham, ἐλάλησεν (elalēsen) can be translated in context “as he promised.” God keeps his word.
Grk “fathers.”
Grk “his seed” (an idiom for offspring or descendants).

will provide a family and a nation for the Messiah. Jesus is the fulfillment of "the seed" of Abraham
(cf. Rom. 2:28-20; Gal. 3:15-19).

verses.zh: 马利亚和伊利莎白同住，约有三个月，就回家去了。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] Mary stayed with Elizabeth[NOTE:2] about three months[NOTE:3] and then returned to her home.
notes: Grk “And.” Here (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the conclusion of the topic.
Grk “her”; the referent (Elizabeth) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
As is typical with Luke the timing is approximate (about three months), not specific.
verses.commentary: 1:56 "then returned to her home" Obviously to face ridicule. Belief always costs in a fallen world!

verses.zh: 伊利莎白的产期到了，就生了一个儿子。
verses.en: Now the time came[NOTE:1] for Elizabeth to have her baby,[NOTE:2] and she gave birth to a son.
notes: Grk “the time was fulfilled.”
The words “her baby” are not in the Greek text, but have been supplied for clarity.
verses.commentary:
1:57 For Jews the birth of a child, especially a son, was a blessing from God. Elizabeth had been
childless for so long and now had delivered a healthy boy!

verses.zh: 邻里亲族听见主向她大施怜悯，就和她一同欢乐。
verses.en: Her[NOTE:1] neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown[NOTE:2] great mercy to her, and they rejoiced[NOTE:3] with her.
notes: Grk “And her.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “had magnified his mercy with her.”
The verb συνέχαιρον (sunechairon) is an imperfect and could be translated as an ingressive force, “they began to rejoice.”

verses.zh: 到了第八日，他们来要给孩子行割礼，并要照他父亲的名字叫他撒迦利亚。
verses.en: On[NOTE:1] the eighth day[NOTE:2] they came to circumcise the child, and they wanted to name[NOTE:3] him Zechariah after his father.
notes: Grk “And it happened that.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
They were following OT law (Lev 12:3) which prescribed that a male child was to be circumcised on the eighth day.
This could be understood as a conative imperfect, expressing an unrealized desire (“they were trying to name him”). It has been given more of a voluntative nuance in the translation.
verses.commentary:
1:59 "on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child" This was practiced by all of Israel's neighbors
except the Philistines (Greek Aegean people). For most cultures it was usually a rite of passage into manhood,
but not for Israel. It was instead an initiation rite into the covenant People. It was a sign of a special
faith relationship with YHWH (Gen. 17:9-14). Each Patriarch circumcised his own sons (i.e., acted as priest
for his own family). Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 214, says the rite of
circumcision connected the rite of blood-shedding with the act of circumcision. Blood was connected to

- covenant forming (cf. Gen. 15:17)

- covenant breaking (cf. Gen. 2:17)

- covenant redemption (cf. Isaiah 53)

The eighth day was the set time for male Jews to have the foreskin of their penises removed
(cf. Lev. 12:3; Gen. 17:12). It was so important that even if the eighth day occurred on the Sabbath the ritual
was still performed.

verses.zh: 他母亲说：「不可！要叫他约翰。」
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] his mother replied,[NOTE:2] “No! He must be named[NOTE:3] John.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “And,” but with clearly contrastive emphasis in context.
Grk “his mother answering, said.” The combination of participle and finite verb is redundant in English and has been simplified to “replied” in the translation.
This future passive indicative verb has imperatival force and thus has been translated “he must be named.”
“No! He must be named John.” By insisting on the name specified by the angel, Elizabeth (v. 60) and Zechariah (v. 63) have learned to obey God (see Luke 1:13).
verses.commentary:
1:60 "he shall be called John" Naming was usually the choice of the father, but for both Jesus
(cf. Matt. 1:21) and John (cf. Luke 1:13) the messenger angel gave their names.

verses.zh: 他们说：「你亲族中没有叫这名字的。」
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] said to her, “But[NOTE:2] none of your relatives bears this name.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “And they.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The word “but” is not in the Greek text but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Grk “There is no one from your relatives who is called by this name.”

verses.zh: 他们就向他父亲打手式，问他要叫这孩子甚么名字。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] they made signs to the baby’s[NOTE:2] father,[NOTE:3] inquiring what he wanted to name his son.[NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the consequential nature of the action described.
Grk “his”; the referent (the baby) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The crowd was sure there had been a mistake, so they appealed to the child’s father. But custom was not to be followed here, since God had spoken. The fact they needed to signal him (made signs) shows that he was deaf as well as unable to speak.
Grk “what he might wish to call him.”

verses.zh: 他要了一块写字的板，就写上，说：「他的名字是约翰。」他们便都希奇。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] asked for a writing tablet[NOTE:2] and wrote,[NOTE:3] “His name is John.” And they were all amazed.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “And he.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The writing tablet requested by Zechariah would have been a wax tablet.
Grk “and wrote, saying.” The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant in English and has not been translated.
The response, they were all amazed, expresses a mixture of surprise and reflection in this setting where they were so certain of what the child’s name would be.

verses.zh: 撒迦利亚的口立时开了，舌头也舒展了，就说出话来，称颂　神。
verses.en: Immediately[NOTE:1] Zechariah’s[NOTE:2] mouth was opened and his tongue[NOTE:3] released,[NOTE:4] and he spoke, blessing God.
notes: Grk “And immediately.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “his”; the referent (Zechariah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The mention of both mouth and tongue here is a figure called zeugma and emphasizes that the end of the temporary judgment came instantly and fully upon Zechariah’s expression of faith in naming the child. He had learned to trust and obey God during his short period of silence. He had learned from his trial.
“Released” is implied; in the Greek text both στόμα (stoma) and γλῶσσα (glōssa) are subjects of ἀνεῴχθη (aneōchthē), but this would be somewhat redundant in English.

verses.zh: 周围居住的人都惧怕；这一切的事就传遍了犹太的山地。
verses.en: All[NOTE:1] their neighbors were filled with fear, and throughout the entire hill country of Judea all these things were talked about.
notes: Grk “And all.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.sn Fear is the emotion that comes when one recognizes something unusual, even supernatural, has taken place.

verses.zh: 凡听见的人都将这事放在心里，说：「这个孩子将来怎么样呢？因为有主与他同在。」
verses.en: All[NOTE:1] who heard these things[NOTE:2] kept them in their hearts,[NOTE:3] saying, “What then will this child be?”[NOTE:4] For the Lord’s hand[NOTE:5] was indeed with him.
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style. A new sentence was begun at this point in the translation because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence.
Grk “heard”; the referent (these things, from the previous verse) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “heart.” The term “heart” (καρδία, kardia) could also be translated as “mind,” or “thoughts,” and the entire phrase be rendered as “kept them in mind,” “thought about,” or the like. But the immediate context is clearly emotive, suggesting that much more is at work than merely the mental processes of thinking or reasoning about “these things.” There is a sense of joy and excitement (see the following question, “What then will this child be?”) and even fear. Further, the use of καρδία in 1:66 suggests connections with the same term in 2:19 where deep emotion is being expressed as well. Therefore, recognizing both the dramatic nature of the immediate context and the literary connections to 2:19, the translation renders the term in 1:66 as “hearts” to capture both the cognitive and emotive aspects of the people’s response.
Or “what manner of child will this one be?”
The reference to the Lord’s hand indicates that the presence, direction, and favor of God was with him (Acts 7:9b).
verses.commentary:
1:66 "For the hand of the Lord was certainly with him" Luke adds these personal comments several times
(cf. Luke 2:50; 3:15; 7:39; 16:14; 20:20; 23:12).

This was a Semitic idiom for God's presence, power, and plan for individuals who become part of
His design for the Kingdom (cf. 1 Chr. 28:19; Ezek. 1:3). By analogy it would apply to the mindset and
worldview of all believers. God is with us, for us, and has a plan and purpose for our lives.

notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

Prophesied. The reference to prophecy reflects that Zechariah is enabled by the Spirit to speak God’s will. He does so in this case through a praise psalm, which calls for praise and then gives the reason why God should be praised. tn Grk “and he prophesied, saying.” The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant and has not been translated.

active in the world before Pentecost. Be careful about making too radical a distinction between the OT actions
of the Spirit and the NT actions of the Spirit. The difference is in the NT personification of the Spirit,
not His powerful presence and actions.

verses.zh: 主―以色列的　神是应当称颂的！因他眷顾他的百姓，为他们施行救赎，
verses.en: “Blessed[NOTE:1] be the Lord God of Israel, because he has come to help[NOTE:2] and has redeemed[NOTE:3] his people.
notes: The traditional name of this psalm, the “Benedictus,” comes from the Latin wording of the start of the hymn (“Blessed be…”).
The verb come to help can refer to a visit, but can also connote concern or assistance (L&N 85.11).

Or “has delivered”; Grk “has accomplished redemption.” sn Has redeemed is a reference to redemption, but it anticipates the total release into salvation that the full work of Messiah will bring for Israel. This involves both spiritual and material benefits eventually.

1:68-70 Zacharias, a Levite and father of John the Baptist, gave thanks to "the Lord God of Israel" for
sending His promised Messiah. The context does not mention his own son (i.e., John) until Luke 1:76-77. Zacharias, who
could now speak, gave a psalm of thanksgiving to YHWH for the salvation He had promised and now brought in His
Messiah (cf. Eph. 1:3-12; 2:8-10).

1:68 "Blessed" This is the Greek word eulogeō. See note at Luke 1:45. The Latin form of this term
is the origin of the title of this psalm, "Benedictus."

▣ "the Lord God of Israel" This phrase contains a Greek translation of the two most common
names for Israel's Deity.

- "Lord" reflects YHWH of Exod. 3:14, which denotes God as Savior, Redeemer, and Covenant-making God (i.e., Genesis 2).

- "God" reflects the general name for God, Elohim (cf. Gen. 1:1), which denotes God as
creator, provider, and sustainer of all life on this planet.

The creator and redeeming God reveals Himself to the world through His dealings
with Abraham and his descendants (cf. Genesis 12;15;17). Israel will be the source of God's promised Messiah.

verses.zh: 在他仆人大卫家中，为我们兴起了拯救的角，
verses.en: For[NOTE:1] he has raised up[NOTE:2] a horn of salvation[NOTE:3] for us in the house of his servant David,[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “and,” but specifying the reason for the praise in the psalm.
The phrase raised up means for God to bring someone significant onto the scene of history.

The horn of salvation is a figure that refers to the power of Messiah and his ability to protect, as the horn refers to what an animal uses to attack and defend (Pss 75:4-5, 10; 148:14; 2 Sam 22:3). Thus the meaning of the figure is “a powerful savior.”
In the house of his servant David is a reference to Messiah’s Davidic descent. Zechariah is more interested in Jesus than his own son John at this point.
verses.commentary:
1:69 "horn of salvation" In the OT animal's horns were a symbol of that animal's power (cf. Deut. 33:17;
Ps. 92:10; Zech. 1:18-21). It became idiomatic to describe the power of the wicked (cf. Ps. 75:10) and the righteous
(cf. 1 Sam. 2:1; Ps. 75:10; 89:17; 148:14).

This cultural idiom came to be used for the efficacious power of the altar of sacrifice
(cf. Exod. 27:2; 30:10; 1 Kgs. 1:50; 2:28). From this developed the concept of God as the efficacious
protector of one's salvation (cf. 2 Sam. 22:2; Ps. 18:2).

Here, it is used of the promised Davidic Messiah (cf. 2 Sam. 7:12-17; Ps. 132:17; Ezek. 29:21;
the lineage of both Mary and Joseph).

▣ "in the house of David His servant" This phrase brings several OT connotations.

- The key term is "house" and the key context is 2 Samuel 7, where it refers to one's genealogy. From this Messianic promise
comes Ps. 132:17 and Isa. 11:1. The Messiah will be from

- the tribe of Judah (cf. Genesis 49)

- the family of Jesse (cf. Matt. 1:1; Luke 1:32; John 7:42; Acts 13:23; Rom. 1:3; Rev. 22:16)

- "Servant" was an OT title of honor used of Moses and Joshua (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT).

verses.en: as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from long ago,[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “from the ages,” “from eternity.”
verses.commentary:

inspires Scripture. This is the NT affirmation of the inspiration and relevance of OT prophecy (cf. Rom. 1:2; 3:21;
16:26). It is also an affirmation of the personality of the Spirit, which is a unique emphasis of the NT. See
Millard J. Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd Ed., pp 875-878.

verses.zh: 拯救我们脱离仇敌和一切恨我们之人的手，

verses.zh: 向我们列祖施怜悯，记念他的圣约―

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO LUKE 1

- Luke the Historian

- Luke 1:1-4 has several rare Greek words that relate to Hellenistic histography. Luke is trying
to express his purpose of accurately recording what his research discovered about Jesus' life
and ministry. Luke was a well educated citizen of the first century Greco-Roman world.

- The problem about Luke's Greek orientation has to do with the nature of Greek history. Often
it was very selective and written more for entertainment and propaganda than modern history. Luke
uses Hellenistic terms to describe his methods, but records Jesus' life in a Hebrew historical fashion.
The best historians in the Ancient Near East (i.e., most accurate) were Hittites and Hebrews. See

SPECIAL TOPIC: OT HISTORIOGRAPHY COMPARED WITH CONTEMPORARY NEAR EASTERN CULTURES

- The real question is what is history? Modern western history is chronological and cause/effect
driven. Yet even modern history is significantly colored by the perspectives of those who write it and why! History,
by its very nature, is a biased selection and description of past events.

- Luke's Gospel is not modern history or biography, but it is good
and true history. The four Gospels are, in reality, gospel tracts, written for evangelistic purposes and
targeting selected groups. Events and their relationship to each other are not necessarily chronologically
arranged but interpreted for maximum impact. This is not to imply they are concoctions or fabrications,
but they are eastern, not western; they are theological as well as historical. Different does not mean bad or false!

See Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read The Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 127-148.

- Luke has used the best traditions of his day to present Jesus Christ as God's promised Messiah, sent to
redeem all humanity. He is surely influenced by Paul's theology (i.e., the Gentile mission). Luke is writing to
convert Gentiles (as well as encourage believers), not just to historically inform them.

- The four Gospels are different, very different, yet they are true-true eyewitness accounts,
true summaries of Jesus' words and activities-but they are not modern histories. Their differences
speak of their genuineness

- Luke clearly wants to put Jesus' life and ministry into a Palestinian and Roman historical framework.

- a vision of Zacharias in reign of Herod, King of Judea (cf. Luke 1:5)

- birth connected to a decree of Caesar Augustus (cf. Luke 2:1)

- birth connected to Quirinius' presence in Syria (cf. Luke 2:2)
